## Overview

multiScaleR is an R package to identify the scale of effect of spatial environmental variables in regression analyses.

Functions to simulate data with known scales of effect are included with this package.

## Installation

Install the CRAN release with:

```{r cran-install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("multiScaleR")
```

Install the latest build from R-universe with:

```{r r-universe-install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(
  "multiScaleR",
  repos = c("https://wpeterman.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org")
)
```

R-universe rebuilds multiScaleR from the `master` branch on GitHub whenever that branch changes. This version can
therefore be newer than the CRAN release. R-universe provides precompiled Windows and macOS binaries with the
vignettes already built, so this route does not require Rtools.

If installing from GitHub on Windows, you may need Rtools to compile the package from source. Choose the Rtools release that matches your version of R and follow the installation instructions at <https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/>.

Then execute the following commands in R:
```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Install 'remotes' package, if needed
if (!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("remotes", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
}

remotes::install_github("wpeterman/multiScaleR", 
                        build_vignettes = TRUE) # Install & build vignette

library(multiScaleR) # Load the package
```

## Bayesian scale estimation

Estimate one shared scale per landscape predictor or model scales as a
function of measured covariates and groups. Use `method = "slice"` for full
posterior sampling without a Stan toolchain. Install `posterior` to assess
chain mixing and simulation precision.

```{r bayesian-workflow, eval=FALSE}
check_bayes_setup(method = "slice")
vignette("v13-bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR")
# Before fitting, simulate_bayes_prior() checks a prepared model's implications.

fit <- multiScale_bayes(
  counts ~ site + land1 + land2, kernel_inputs, dat,
  family = "poisson", method = "slice", seed = 5211
)
summary(fit)$diagnostics             # inspect chain mixing
diagnose_bayes_scales(fit)$quantiles  # check simulation error of scale quantiles
posterior_scales(fit)                # one distance and credible interval per layer
plot(fit)
```

The vignette displays actual fitted results from an artificial annual-map
example, including shared and independent controls, predictive checks and prior
sensitivity. Compact stored draws let you read it without rerunning MCMC.
NUTS sampling uses RTMB, tmbstan, rstan, and posterior.
Preparation can be checked without them using `method = "prepare"`.
`predict_scales()` predicts scales for unobserved years. `predict()` and
`simulate()` accept new observations and matching prepared landscapes, with
explicit choices for new year and site effects. Read
`vignette("v14-bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR")` for a worked forecast,
shared group effects and joint totals. Future responses require a response
formula that supports unseen years; a fixed year factor cannot supply a new
coefficient. Approximation methods remain experimental,
and numerical convergence does not establish interval accuracy.
For the alternative computations, actual matched outputs and interpretation
of their numerical checks, read
`vignette("v15-bayesian-computation", package = "multiScaleR")`.

## Kernel distance reporting

Starting with version 0.7.4, `kernel_dist()`, kernel plots,
and the selected summary distance default to `dimension = "2d"`: the radius
containing the requested share of an ideal kernel's total weight on a plane.
At 90%, a Gaussian kernel with sigma = 300 m has a planar radius of about
644 m, compared with the original line-based distance of about 493 m.
Raster edges, missing cells, cell geometry, and `max_D` can change the weight
actually retained at a site.

Set `dimension = "1d"` in `kernel_dist()`, `plot_kernel()`, `plot(fit)`, or
`summary(fit)` to restore the original definition. Summary `opt_dist` and
`opt_distance` follow that selection; `opt_dist_1d` and `opt_dist_2d` always
identify the two definitions explicitly. This reporting switch does not change
the fitted sigma, coefficients, or likelihood. Simulation extents, projection
windows, and stored optimization warnings retain their historical 1D cutoffs.
See `vignette("v02-user-guide", package = "multiScaleR")` for interpretation
and migration examples.

## Marginal effects for unmarked models

Version 0.7.4 fixes marginal-effect plots for models with factors such as
`Year`, extra site-ID columns, and repeated site-year rows linked by `join_by`.
Predictors are recovered from the state or abundance formula. Numeric
predictors are held at their observed means and categorical predictors at
their first observed values in other panels. Factors receive a point and
confidence interval for each observed level.

For random-effects models, plots set site effects to zero explicitly.
These are conditional predictions, not averages over years, sites, or the
random-effect distribution. Their intervals are conditional on the selected
scale. See `?plot_marginal_effects` for supported prediction types and factor
contrast handling. Existing fitted objects can be plotted without rerunning
scale optimization.
